title: Assess Work Area and Equipment for Compliance with Regulations

lessons.title: Pre-operational checks of the inspection area
lessons.html:
Why check before slaughter starts

Before the first animal is slaughtered, the meat examiner checks that the slaughter hall and inspection points are clean and fit for use. The Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000 and its regulations require abattoirs to keep facilities hygienic, and the abattoir's hygiene management system will describe a pre-operational inspection. If the area is not ready, slaughter must not start until it is put right.

What to check in the slaughter hall

  • Floors, walls and ceilings are clean, with no meat scraps, blood or fat left from the previous day.
  • No condensation dripping from ceilings or rails onto where carcasses will hang.
  • Drains are open and covered with grids, and there is no standing water.
  • Lighting at inspection points is bright enough to see lesions clearly, with light covers intact so broken glass cannot fall onto meat.
  • No pests, droppings or signs of birds, rats or flies.
  • Doors and screens close properly.

The inspection points

Each inspection point (head, offal, carcass) needs its own hand wash basin with hot water, soap and paper towels, operated by knee or foot, and a knife steriliser with hot water. There must be enough space for the examiner to stand safely and see all surfaces. A detention rail must be available, separated from the main line, so suspect carcasses can be moved aside.

Recording the check

Use the pre-operational checklist. Mark each item as acceptable or not acceptable, write down what was wrong, and record the corrective action and the time it was fixed. Sign the sheet. Hand any problems to the abattoir supervisor and check again before giving permission to start.

lessons.title: Checking equipment and personal hygiene
lessons.html:
Equipment that touches meat

Every piece of equipment that touches meat must be clean, in good repair and made of material that can be cleaned, such as stainless steel or food-grade plastic. Wooden handles, rust and cracked plastic hide bacteria.

Equipment checklist

  • Knives and steels: sharp, clean, with sound handles. A blunt knife causes poor incisions and accidents.
  • Knife sterilisers: full of clean water at the operating temperature set in the abattoir's procedures. Check with a calibrated thermometer, not by hand.
  • Hooks, gambrels and rails: clean, no rust or grease that could drip on carcasses.
  • Offal trays and tables: clean and sanitised, and synchronised with the carcass line where this is used.
  • Saws and splitting equipment: clean, guards in place, sterilised between carcasses.
  • Condemned material containers: clearly marked, lockable or kept separate, and not used for anything else.
  • Thermometers and scales: calibrated, with records of calibration.

Personal hygiene and protective clothing

The examiner sets the example. Check that you and the workers wear clean overalls, aprons, gumboots and hair nets or helmets. Remove jewellery and watches. Cuts on hands must be covered with a waterproof, coloured plaster and gloves. Anyone with diarrhoea, vomiting or an infected wound must report to the supervisor and must not handle meat. Wash hands when entering the hall, after using the toilet and whenever they become dirty.

Safety

Wear a chain mail glove or apron where your procedures require it. Never leave knives lying on the floor or on carcasses. Walk carefully on wet floors and wear boots with non-slip soles.

lessons.title: Dealing with non-compliance
lessons.html:
When something is not right

Finding a problem is only half the job. You must make sure it is fixed and recorded. Problems are often called non-conformances.

Steps to follow

  1. Identify the problem clearly, for example: steriliser at point 2 not hot enough.
  2. Decide how serious it is. Could it contaminate meat right now? If yes, slaughter must not start or must stop at that point.
  3. Inform the abattoir supervisor or foreman and agree on the corrective action.
  4. Check that the action was done, for example re-cleaning the area or repairing the steriliser.
  5. Record the problem, the action, the time and the people involved.
  6. If the same problem keeps coming back, report it to the veterinarian or management so the root cause can be fixed.

Examples

ProblemTypical action
Meat scraps on the offal tableRe-clean and sanitise before use
No soap at a hand basinRefill before work starts
Broken light cover above the lineReplace; check for glass on meat surfaces
Rust on rail above carcassesClean and schedule maintenance

Working with the abattoir

Be firm but respectful. The aim is safe meat, not blame. Explain what the rule requires and why. Good records show auditors from provincial veterinary services that problems are found and fixed.

Key points

  • Do a pre-operational check before slaughter starts and record it.
  • Every inspection point needs a hand wash basin and a working knife steriliser.
  • Equipment must be clean, in good repair and made of cleanable material.
  • Sick workers or workers with uncovered wounds must not handle meat.
  • Record every non-conformance and check that the corrective action was done.
